extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for corporate apology and crisis-management after a racially insensitive ad/social-media incident, with emphasis on actions a fashion brand should take to contain reputational damage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distance brand from offending individual
rubrics_metrics.description: “The best decision the brand can make now is to distance itself from the man [Gabbana]. Show that the brand does not share the racist and prejudiced thinking of its co-founder and is committed to providing the best products and service to everyone, everywhere.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publicly separate the company identity from the remarks/behaviour of a named founder or spokesperson to limit association; communicate that the brand’s values differ from the individual's conduct and emphasize ongoing commitment to all customers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural sensitivity in advertising/content
rubrics_metrics.description: “They should’ve been more sensitive with the reactions of the citizens of China towards the ads.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid tone-deaf imagery or jokes that appropriate or stereotype another culture (e.g., chopsticks/cannoli jokes). Vet creative concepts for cultural misinterpretation before release; involve cultural consultants or local stakeholders in review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timely response to backlash
rubrics_metrics.description: “It’s too late to ‘show their love to China’ when all the damages are done. It sounded like a last-ditch effort to defend their brand.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respond quickly — delays reduce effectiveness of damage control. Proactive, timely communications are more credible than reactive, last-minute attempts to stem outrage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity and credibility of apology (avoid weak excuses)
rubrics_metrics.description: “The apology and hacking excuse, unfortunately, gained almost no traction because of Gabbana’s history of offending others.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure apologies are genuine and backed by credible facts; avoid implausible or easily-dismissed explanations (e.g., claiming an account was hacked) especially when prior behaviour undermines trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sever or limit relationships with problematic ambassadors/clients
rubrics_metrics.description: “Morally, I wouldn’t work with a client who’s racist. And if it happens that a client of mine turned out to be one, the easy thing to do is to cut ties with the least financial exposure possible.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider terminating contracts or partnerships with brand ambassadors, influencers, or partners whose actions create reputational risk; do so strategically to minimize financial/legal exposure while signaling values alignment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use simple, sincere messaging to show respect
rubrics_metrics.description: “If the brand claims it wants to show its love for China, wouldn’t it be more genuine to post a simple video of the designers sending their love to China to create bigger anticipation for their show?”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When expressing solidarity or affection for a market/community, prefer straightforward, sincere content over elaborate or gimmicky material. Simple personal messages can feel more authentic and defuse criticism if deployed appropriately and timely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monitor and respect consumer sentiment; prepare for retail fallout
rubrics_metrics.description: Retailers around the world have pulled the brand’s products... customers in mainland China and Hong Kong are returning their D&G items.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipate that consumer outrage can trigger retailer delistings, returns, and lost sales; actively monitor partner reactions and have contingency plans for distribution, inventory, and retail relationships.

rubrics_metrics.name: Past behaviour shapes present credibility
rubrics_metrics.description: “Gabbana’s history of offending others... With a brand so impervious to controversies, the designers have been accused of just crying wolf.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that a history of controversial statements reduces the effectiveness of apologies and explanations; ongoing behavioural patterns must be addressed (e.g., substantive change, third-party verification) to rebuild trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manage operational and regulatory risks from social-media conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: “Curious what the Chinese government will think... considering how strict they are on who to allow to enter the country on work visas based on a thorough social media background checks.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for secondary consequences of online behaviour: cancelled shows, revoked visas/work permits, casting withdrawals, and government scrutiny. Implement social-media policies and background checks for key personnel to mitigate such risks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public apology should express respect and remorse
rubrics_metrics.description: Founders said: “We want to apologise if we have made mistakes in interpreting your culture. We have always loved China… and certainly we still have much to learn.” “We offer our sincerest apologies to Chinese people worldwide.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Craft apologies that explicitly acknowledge harm, express remorse, and affirm respect for the affected community. Avoid conditional phrasing that minimizes responsibility; follow words with concrete corrective actions where possible.
